Apple yesterday showcased what it called "stunning evidence" based on a forensic analysis of a MacBook belonging to former employee Chang Liu, who has since moved to OpenAI. Apple alleges the two former employees stole trade secrets related to, among other things, hardware design.

The AI company fired back in its own legal filings, calling the whole thing a "mess of Apple's own making."

The ongoing lawsuit seeks to determine whether Chang Liu and Tang Tan took confidential information with them when they left Apple to help OpenAI develop AI hardware devices after their departure. The complaint specifically notes that the two engineers downloaded confidential engineering files after leaving the iPhone maker.

Apple was granted access to one of Chang Liu's MacBooks for forensic analysis to determine whether it contained evidence of unauthorized access to company intellectual property. Apple told the court in a filing yesterday that it had found four pieces of "stunning" evidence supporting its claims.

OpenAI's own filings submitted the same day were equally blunt in their language, Reuters reported.

Top comment from visegripmikey

The failure here is an unaccounted-for "man in the middle." In IT terms, this is PBKAC (Problem Between Keyboard and Chair). Employees agree to information security terms when they join. So long as they don't violate those terms, they're fine. As an analogy, in a track event like the 100m sprint, the rules say stay in your lane. Even though that line is just paint that anyone could easily cross, step into someone else's lane and you're disqualified.

The filings specifically pointed to three factors that contributed to the problem:

  • Apple encourages employees to use personal iCloud accounts to access internal Apple documents
  • Departing employees aren't given enough time to return company devices, files, and complete work handovers
  • After former employees leave, their former colleagues contact them for help and ask them to access company data

9to5Mac Take

On the surface, Apple's filing yesterday does indeed look pretty damning. OpenAI doesn't seem to dispute that the company used Apple's confidential information, instead claiming the iPhone maker failed to properly secure it.

However, and while I'm not a lawyer, I understand this may be a key argument — because a company can only designate something as a trade secret if it takes proper steps to protect it. If OpenAI can demonstrate Apple failed to do so, then even if the use of the information is true, the AI company could potentially still win.
